message:
QUESTION:
Did the 1 June move to a new content delivery network (CDN) improve the site's conversion rate, and what is a faster site worth?

DATA:
An online retailer migrated its website to a new content delivery network (CDN) on 1 June. Two weeks before (18-31 May) vs two weeks after (1-14 June):

| Metric | 18-31 May | 1-14 June |
| Sessions | 200,000 | 210,000 |
| Orders | 5,000 | 5,670 |
| Median page load time | 3.2 s | 2.1 s |
| 95th-percentile page load time | 7.5 s | 4.8 s |
| Bounce rate | 48% | 44% |

Conversion = orders / sessions. Page load times come from real-user monitoring across all page views.

Same two calendar periods last year, when there were no site or infrastructure changes: conversion 2.4% (18-31 May) and 2.6% (1-14 June).

The retailer's conversion rate rises every year in early June when the summer ranges launch. This year the summer ranges again launched on 1 June. No other site changes were made between 18 May and 14 June.

KNOWN FLAWS:
F1. [calculation] The reduction is (7.5 − 4.8) / 7.5 = 36%. 56% comes from dividing the 2.7 s fall by the new value (4.8). The draft's claim that the slowest experiences 'improved even more' than the median (34%) is barely true at 36%. CORRECTION: 95th percentile fell by 36%, similar to the median's 34%.
F2. [misreport] The data show bounce rate fell from 48% to 44%. CORRECTION: A 4-point (8% relative) fall in bounce rate.
F3. [method] Ignores the seasonal baseline: the same calendar periods last year, with no site changes, show the same 0.2-point rise (2.4% to 2.6%) from the summer range launch, which happened again on 1 June. CORRECTION: Year-over-year difference-in-differences: (2.70 − 2.50) − (2.6 − 2.4) = 0.0 points. There is no detectable conversion effect of the CDN.
F4. [inference] Derives a linear causal 'value per second' from one confounded before/after comparison and extrapolates it beyond the observed range. CORRECTION: The data support no value-per-second estimate (the seasonally adjusted effect is about zero). A randomised latency experiment would be needed.

EXTENSIONS:
- Run a statistical check on the raw conversion change (2.50% vs 2.70%, z of about 4) and contrast it with the seasonally adjusted comparison, showing that a highly significant before/after change can be entirely seasonal.
- Check whether the sessions increase (+5%) is also seasonal, using last year's session counts for the same periods, which the analyst should request.
- Segment by device or connection type: speed gains typically matter most on mobile and slow connections, so an effect masked in the aggregate could appear there (data would be needed).

FINAL VERSION:
# CDN migration: performance and conversion impact

**Summary.** The 1 June CDN migration made the site much faster. It did **not** produce a measurable lift in conversion.

- Conversion rose 0.2 points. It also rose about 0.2 points over the same dates last year, when nothing on the site changed. That rise is the usual early-June summer-range effect.
- The estimate is imprecise. Sampling noise alone allows a CDN effect anywhere from about −0.14 to +0.14 points. Rounding in last year's figures and year-to-year seasonal variation widen that range further.
- A small effect is therefore not ruled out, and it could still be worth money.
- This data cannot tell us what a second of load time is worth.
- Settling either question needs unrounded prior-year data and a properly sized controlled test.

**Background.** The site moved to a new CDN on 1 June. This note compares the two weeks before (18–31 May) with the two weeks after (1–14 June).

- Load times come from real-user monitoring (RUM) across all page views.
- Figures are site-wide totals. Device and channel splits are not included.
- The summer ranges launched on 1 June, as they do every year. No other site changes were made between 18 May and 14 June.

## Speed

Load times fell sharply, very likely because of the CDN.

| Metric | 18–31 May | 1–14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median load time | 3.2 s | 2.1 s | −1.1 s (−34%) |
| 95th-percentile load time | 7.5 s | 4.8 s | −2.7 s (−36%) |

- The slowest loads improved by about the same proportion as typical loads, and by much more in absolute terms.
- No other site changes were made. Seasonal shifts in traffic, page mix and cache hit rates could still have played a small part. Prior-year load times for the same dates would confirm this.
- If RUM previously missed slow loads that users abandoned, the true improvement is larger than shown.

## Engagement

These changes coincide with both the CDN change and the summer launch. Without prior-year bounce, session and order counts, we cannot yet say how much of each change is seasonal.

- Bounce rate fell from 48% to 44% (−4 points).
- Sessions rose 5%, from 200,000 to 210,000.
- Orders rose 13.4%, from 5,000 to 5,670. That is a rise from about 357 to about 405 a day: roughly 48 extra orders a day, or 670 over the fortnight.

## Conversion

Conversion (orders ÷ sessions) rose from 2.50% to 2.70%.

| | 18–31 May | 1–14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Last year (no site changes) | 2.4% | 2.6% | +0.2 pts (rounded) |
| This year (CDN migration 1 June) | 2.50% | 2.70% | +0.20 pts |
| **Difference-in-differences (estimate)** | | | **≈ 0 pts** |

- Last year's seasonal pattern predicts what this June's conversion would have been with no site change. Applied additively, the prediction is 2.50% + 0.2 = 2.70%. Applied proportionally, it is 2.50% × 2.6/2.4 ≈ 2.71%.
- Actual conversion was 2.70%. Either method therefore attributes essentially the whole rise to seasonality.
- The extra orders came from more sessions plus the seasonal conversion uplift. On current evidence they should not be credited to the CDN.

**How uncertain is "≈ 0"?** Three sources of uncertainty add together:

- **Sampling.** Each period's conversion rate has a standard error of about 0.035 pts. The estimate combines four periods. Assuming last year's traffic was similar, that gives a standard error of about 0.07 pts and a 95% interval of roughly **−0.14 to +0.14 pts**. This is optimistic, because repeat visitors make sessions less than independent.
- **Rounding.** Last year's 2.4% and 2.6% are rounded. The true seasonal rise could be anywhere from about 0.1 to 0.3 pts. That alone moves the estimate by up to ±0.1 pts.
- **Seasonal variability.** The size of the summer uplift varies from year to year. A single prior year cannot measure that variation.

**Would an effect of that size matter?** At current traffic, each 0.1 pt of conversion is about 210 orders a fortnight. Multiplying by average order value gives the revenue. An effect too small for this data to detect could still be commercially meaningful. That is the case for a proper test.

## Session counting: a caveat that cuts both ways

- **The concern.** Before the migration, users may have left slow pages before analytics loaded, so those visits went unrecorded. The faster site now records them. Such visits are mostly low-intent, so they raise sessions and lower measured conversion.
- **What it can and cannot hide.** Orders are presumably counted server-side, so they are unaffected. This effect can therefore hide a CDN effect on conversion, but not on orders.
- **How to check.** Compare this year's order growth (+13.4%) with last year's growth for the same dates. If this year's is clearly higher, the CDN may have lifted sales even though conversion looks flat.
- **The counter-evidence.** Recovered sessions would mostly be single-page bounces, which should push the bounce rate up. Instead it fell 4 points. Either few sessions were recovered, or the CDN reduced bounces enough to outweigh them. Prior-year bounce rates would show which.

## What is a second worth?

This data cannot answer that. Dividing 0.2 points by 1.1 seconds gives "0.18 points per second," and that figure is invalid for three reasons:

- the 0.2 points is seasonal, not a speed effect;
- a single before/after comparison cannot separate speed from everything else that changed on 1 June;
- speed gains typically show diminishing returns, so a further second below 2.1 s would not be worth the same as the first.

## Measuring it properly

Any test must be sized around a stated minimum detectable effect (MDE), meaning the smallest effect worth finding. The table below assumes about 15,000 sessions a day, 2.7% conversion, 80% power and α = 0.05.

| Design | Sessions in smaller arm | Smallest detectable effect |
|---|---|---|
| 5% holdback, 3 weeks | ~16,000 | ~0.37 pts (+14%) |
| 50/50, 3 weeks | ~158,000 | ~0.16 pts (+6%) |
| 50/50, ~8 weeks | ~410,000 | ~0.10 pts (+4%) |

A 5% holdback would almost certainly come back null even if a commercially meaningful effect exists. Users should be randomised rather than sessions, so that each visitor sees one consistent experience. That increases the required sample further.

1. **CDN holdback test (answers the CDN question).**
   - Randomly assign users to the old or new CDN.
   - Choose the MDE using average order value, then pick the split and duration needed to reach it.
   - Compare orders per user as well as conversion. This avoids the session-counting problem.
   - Randomisation controls for seasonality, so there is no need to wait until after summer.
   - The costs are that the holdback group misses any CDN benefit during the test, and the old CDN must stay available.
2. **Latency injection test (values speed in general).**
   - Randomly add delay for some users, for example +0.5 s and +1 s.
   - This shows how conversion changes with each increment of delay, which is what speed is worth.
   - The same sizing applies. A small, short test will be too small to detect a realistic effect.
   - Deliberately slowing the site costs revenue and goodwill, so weigh that cost against the MDE.
   - Running the test outside the summer launch makes the results more representative of the rest of the year.

A cheap but weak alternative is to compare conversion across session load-time bands. Treat the results as indicative only. Slow sessions are heavily confounded with device, network and page type, even after controls.

## Next steps

1. **Priority:** pull unrounded prior-year sessions, orders, bounce rate and load times for both periods, plus conversion for two or three further years. This data would:
   - check this year's order growth against last year's;
   - show why the bounce rate fell;
   - remove the rounding error;
   - show how much the seasonal uplift varies from year to year.
2. Agree an MDE using average order value. Then decide whether a holdback test of the required size is worth its cost.
3. Do not use a points-per-second figure in business cases until it has been measured experimentally.
4. Judge the CDN on what it has been shown to deliver: faster load times, plus cost, reliability and operational benefits.
5. Monitor load times weekly through the summer traffic peak. Compare conversion against the prior-year seasonal pattern rather than against May.
6. Pull device and channel splits to check whether any segment shows a lift beyond seasonality.

## Conclusion

The CDN cut median load time by 1.1 s and 95th-percentile load time by 2.7 s. Conversion rose by the same amount as last year's summer-launch increase, so there is no evidence that the faster site improved conversion. The data cannot rule out an effect of roughly 0.15 points either way. Once rounding and seasonal variability are included, the possible effect could be larger. At current traffic, 0.15 points is worth around 300 orders a fortnight. Prior-year data and an adequately sized controlled test are needed to settle whether the CDN lifted sales and what speed is worth.
